notes.summary:
Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together; regression gives an equation to estimate one from the other. Paper 2 asks 8 to 12 questions: the scatter diagram, properties of r, Karl Pearson's r, Spearman's rank correlation, regression coefficients and lines, association of attributes (Yule's Q), and partial and multiple correlation for three variables.

Most computations reduce to a few identities: r = Cov(x, y) ÷ (σxσy), r² = byx × bxy, and both regression lines pass through (x̄, ȳ).

concepts.title: Kinds of correlation and the scatter diagram
concepts.body:
• Positive: both rise together (height and weight). Negative: one rises as the other falls (price and demand).
  • Linear: points lie near a straight line. Non-linear (curvilinear): they follow a curve.
  • Simple: two variables. Partial: two variables with the effect of a third held fixed. Multiple: one variable against two or more together.
  • A scatter diagram plots each (x, y) pair as a dot. Rising band = positive, falling band = negative, round cloud = no correlation, all on a line = perfect correlation.
  • Correlation is not causation. Two variables can move together because of a third factor, or by chance (spurious or nonsense correlation).

concepts.title: Karl Pearson's coefficient r
concepts.body:
• Covariance: Cov(x, y) = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ n = Σxy ÷ n − x̄ȳ.
  • r = Cov(x, y) ÷ (σxσy) = Σdxdy ÷ √(Σdx² × Σdy²), where dx = x − x̄, dy = y − ȳ.
  • Raw-sum form: r = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy] ÷ √{[nΣx² − (Σx)²][nΣy² − (Σy)²]}.

Mini example: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4. dx = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; dy = −2, 0, 1, 0, 1. Σdxdy = 6, Σdx² = 10, Σdy² = 6. r = 6 ÷ √60 = 0.77.

concepts.title: Properties of r
concepts.body:
• −1 ≤ r ≤ +1. r = +1 or −1 means perfect linear relation; r = 0 means no linear relation (a curved relation may still exist).
  • r has no units and is symmetric: rxy = ryx.
  • r does not change with change of origin and scale, except for sign: if u = (x − a)/h and v = (y − b)/k, then ruv = rxy when h and k have the same sign, and −rxy when they have opposite signs.
  • r is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients.
  • If x and y are independent, r = 0, but r = 0 does not prove independence.
  • Coefficient of determination = r². r = 0.8 means 64% of the variation in y is explained by x. Coefficient of non-determination = 1 − r².
  • Probable error PE = 0.6745 × (1 − r²) ÷ √n. If r > 6 PE, r is taken as significant; if r < PE, not significant.
|r|Description
1Perfect
0.75 to 1High
0.5 to 0.75Moderate
below 0.5Low
0No linear correlation

concepts.title: Spearman's rank correlation
concepts.body:
Used for ranks or qualitative data (beauty, honesty) that can be ranked but not measured.

  • ρ = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ [n(n² − 1)], d = difference between the two ranks of each item.
  • Σd = 0 always (a quick check of your ranks).
  • Tied ranks: give each tied item the average of the ranks they share (two items tied for 3rd and 4th both get 3.5). For each tie group of size m, add m(m² − 1) ÷ 12 to Σd².
  • ρ lies between −1 and +1. Ranks in exactly the same order give ρ = 1; in exactly reverse order give ρ = −1.

Mini example: n = 6, Σd² = 14. ρ = 1 − 84 ÷ 210 = 0.6.

Concurrent deviation method: rc = ±√(±(2c − n) ÷ n), where c = number of pairs whose deviations move in the same direction and n = number of pairs of deviations.

concepts.title: Regression coefficients
concepts.body:
• Regression of y on x: y − ȳ = byx(x − x̄), with byx = r σy ÷ σx = Cov(x, y) ÷ σx². It estimates y for a given x.
  • Regression of x on y: x − x̄ = bxy(y − ȳ), with bxy = r σx ÷ σy = Cov(x, y) ÷ σy².
  • r² = byx × bxy, so r = ±√(byx × bxy), taking the common sign of the coefficients.
  • Both coefficients and r have the same sign. Both cannot be greater than 1 in size (their product is at most 1).
  • The AM of the two coefficients is at least r: (byx + bxy) ÷ 2 ≥ r (for positive r).
  • Regression coefficients change with scale but not with origin: if u = (x − a)/h and v = (y − b)/k, then bvu = (h/k) byx.

Mini example: r = 0.5, σx = 3, σy = 6. byx = 0.5 × 6/3 = 1 and bxy = 0.5 × 3/6 = 0.25.

concepts.title: Regression lines
concepts.body:
• There are two lines, y on x and x on y. Both pass through (x̄, ȳ), so solving the two equations together gives the means.
  • If r = ±1 the two lines coincide. If r = 0 they are perpendicular (y = ȳ and x = x̄).
  • The closer the lines, the higher the correlation.
  • Angle between them: tan θ = [(1 − r²) ÷ |r|] × [σxσy ÷ (σx² + σy²)].
  • Which line is which: assume one is y on x (write it as y = … to read byx) and the other is x on y (write as x = … to read bxy). If the product is at most 1, the guess is right; if it is above 1, swap.
  • Standard error of estimate of y: Sy = σy√(1 − r²).

Mini example: lines 8x − 10y + 66 = 0 and 40x − 18y = 214. Solving: x̄ = 13, ȳ = 17. From the first, y = 0.8x + 6.6 so byx = 0.8; from the second, x = 0.45y + 5.35 so bxy = 0.45. r² = 0.36, r = 0.6.

concepts.title: Association of attributes
concepts.body:
For two attributes A and B (say vaccinated and not attacked), write the class frequencies as (AB), (Ab), (aB), (ab), where small letters mean "not".

  • Independent if (AB) = (A)(B) ÷ N. Positively associated if (AB) is greater than this, negatively if less.
  • Yule's coefficient of association: Q = [(AB)(ab) − (Ab)(aB)] ÷ [(AB)(ab) + (Ab)(aB)]. It lies from −1 to +1; Q = 0 means independent.
  • Coefficient of colligation: Y = (1 − √k) ÷ (1 + √k), k = (Ab)(aB) ÷ [(AB)(ab)]. Relation: Q = 2Y ÷ (1 + Y²).
  • Order of a class frequency = number of attributes in it: N is order 0, (A) is order 1, (AB) is order 2. With n attributes there are 3n class frequencies in all.
  • Data are consistent only if no class frequency is negative.

concepts.title: Partial and multiple correlation (three variables)
concepts.body:
• Partial correlation between 1 and 2 with 3 held fixed: r12.3 = (r12 − r13r23) ÷ √[(1 − r13²)(1 − r23²)]. It lies from −1 to +1.
  • Multiple correlation of 1 on 2 and 3: R1.23² = (r12² + r13² − 2r12r13r23) ÷ (1 − r23²). It lies from 0 to 1 and is never less than any simple correlation of 1 with 2 or 3: R1.23 ≥ |r12|, |r13|.
  • If R1.23 = 0, then r12 = r13 = 0. If R1.23 = 1, x1 is an exact linear function of x2 and x3.
  • Multiple regression plane of x1 on x2, x3: x1 = a + b12.3x2 + b13.2x3; b12.3 is a partial regression coefficient.

Mini example: r12 = 0.7, r13 = 0.5, r23 = 0.5. r12.3 = (0.7 − 0.25) ÷ 0.75 = 0.6. R1.23² = (0.49 + 0.25 − 0.35) ÷ 0.75 = 0.52, R1.23 ≈ 0.72.

varieties.name: Scatter diagram and properties of r
varieties.how: r ignores origin and scale; only the signs of the multipliers matter. Opposite signs flip the sign of r.

example.q: r between x and y is 0.6. Find r between u = 2 − 3x and v = 5y + 1.
steps: The added constants 2 and 1 do not affect r.
The multipliers are −3 and 5, which have opposite signs.

varieties.name: Computing Karl Pearson's r
varieties.how: r = Cov(x, y) ÷ (σₓσᵧ). From data, take deviations from the means and use Σdxdy ÷ √(Σdx² Σdy²).

example.q: Cov(x, y) = 12, σₓ = 4 and σᵧ = 5. Find r and the coefficient of determination.
steps: Coefficient of determination = r² = 0.36, so 36% of the variation in y is explained by x.

varieties.name: Spearman's rank correlation
varieties.how: ρ = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ [n(n² − 1)]. With ties, add m(m² − 1)/12 to Σd² for each group of m equal ranks.

example.q: Two judges rank 6 contestants. The sum of squared rank differences is 14. Find the rank correlation coefficient.

varieties.name: Regression coefficients
varieties.how: byx = r σᵧ/σₓ, bxy = r σₓ/σᵧ, r = ±√(byx × bxy) with the common sign.

example.q: The regression coefficients are byx = 0.9 and bxy = 0.4. Find r.
steps: Both coefficients are positive, so r is positive.

varieties.name: Regression lines, means and estimates
varieties.how: Solve both equations for x̄ and ȳ. Read byx and bxy by rewriting each line; if their product exceeds 1, swap the roles.

example.q: The regression lines are 8x − 10y + 66 = 0 and 40x − 18y = 214. Find x̄, ȳ and r.
steps: Take the first as y on x: y = 0.8x + 6.6, so byx = 0.8.
Take the second as x on y: x = 0.45y + 5.35, so bxy = 0.45.
r² = 0.8 × 0.45 = 0.36 ≤ 1, so the guess is right and r = +0.6.

varieties.name: Association of attributes
varieties.how: Q = [(AB)(ab) − (Ab)(aB)] ÷ [(AB)(ab) + (Ab)(aB)]. Positive Q means positive association.

varieties.name: Partial and multiple correlation
varieties.how: r₁₂.₃ = (r₁₂ − r₁₃r₂₃) ÷ √[(1 − r₁₃²)(1 − r₂₃²)]. R₁.₂₃² = (r₁₂² + r₁₃² − 2r₁₂r₁₃r₂₃) ÷ (1 − r₂₃²).

example.q: r₁₂ = 0.7, r₁₃ = 0.5 and r₂₃ = 0.5. Find r₁₂.₃.

tips: r is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients and has their sign.
The two regression lines meet at (x̄, ȳ): solve them as simultaneous equations to get the means.
If the product of the two slopes you read off comes out above 1, you have the lines the wrong way round.
For rank correlation, Σd is always 0; use it to check your ranks before squaring.
r² is the share of variation explained: r = 0.9 explains 81%.
Multiple correlation R₁.₂₃ is between 0 and 1 and never smaller than |r₁₂| or |r₁₃|.
traps: r = 0 means no linear relation, not no relation at all.
Changing origin and scale does not change r, but it does change the regression coefficients (by scale).
byx uses σᵧ on top: byx = r σᵧ/σₓ. Mixing these up is the commonest slip.
Both regression coefficients cannot exceed 1 in size, and they cannot have opposite signs.
In Spearman's formula, n(n² − 1) is n³ − n, not n²(n − 1).

formulas.name: Spearman rank correlation
formulas.expr: ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/[n(n² − 1)];  ties: add m(m² − 1)/12 per tie group

formulas.name: Regression coefficients
formulas.expr: byx = r σᵧ/σₓ,  bxy = r σₓ/σᵧ,  r² = byx × bxy

formulas.name: Regression lines
formulas.expr: y − ȳ = byx(x − x̄);  x − x̄ = bxy(y − ȳ)

questions.q: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation always lies between:
questions.solution: −1 ≤ r ≤ +1. r = +1 is perfect positive and r = −1 perfect negative correlation.

questions.q: The two regression coefficients are b<sub>xy</sub> = 0.8 and b<sub>yx</sub> = 0.2. The correlation coefficient r is:
questions.solution: r = √(b<sub>xy</sub> × b<sub>yx</sub>) = √(0.8 × 0.2) = √0.16 = 0.4. Positive, because both coefficients are positive.

questions.q: For 5 pairs of ranks, Σd² = 10. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is:
r = 0.6, σ<sub>x</sub> = 4 and σ<sub>y</sub> = 8. The regression coefficient of y on x is:
The two regression lines are 3x + 2y = 26 and 6x + y = 31. The means x̄ and ȳ are:
questions.solution:
Both lines pass through (x̄, ȳ). From the second: y = 31 − 6x.
Put in the first: 3x + 2(31 − 6x) = 26 ⇒ 3x + 62 − 12x = 26 ⇒ −9x = −36 ⇒ x = 4.
y = 31 − 24 = 7. So x̄ = 4, ȳ = 7.

questions.q: For the regression lines 3x + 2y = 26 and 6x + y = 31, the correlation coefficient r is:
questions.solution:
Try 3x + 2y = 26 as y on x: y = 13 − 1.5x, so byx = −1.5.
Then 6x + y = 31 as x on y: x = 31/6 − y/6, so bxy = −1/6.
Product = 1.5/6 = 0.25 ≤ 1, so this choice is valid (the other choice gives product 4 > 1).
r = −√0.25 = −0.5 (negative, same sign as the coefficients).

flashcards.back: ±√(byx · bxy), sign same as the coefficients
